newsitem.title: USA: Spy Ames claims did no big damage to United States.
newsitem.headline: Spy Ames claims did no big damage to United States.

text.p: Confessed CIA turncoat Aldrich Ames asserted in remarks aired on Tuesday night that he had done no major damage to U.S. national security despite having told Moscow of as many as 25 spies secretly working for U.S. intelligence agencies.

But in an ABC "Nightline" interview from the federal penitentiary in Allenwood, Pennsylvania, where he is serving a life sentence, Ames acknowledged he had done great damage to the Central Intelligence Agency, where he worked for 31 years.

"I do maintain that no significant damage to our national security interests occurred," he said. "Tremendous damage was done to the agency's institutional framework, the agency's operations and, most importantly, to an awful lot of people."

The ABC interview was tied to the publication of a new book that reported Ames had identified 25 "human assets" to the former KGB Soviet security service, more than twice the number that U.S. officials have acknowledged publicly.

Of those he fingered, at least 10 were later killed or disappeared in what amounted to the CIA's worst known security breach. Ames pleaded guilty to selling Moscow stacks of secrets from 1985 to 1994 for payments totalling more than $2.5 million.
"Nightline" reported that Ames had been placed in "involuntary protective custody" on Monday when he appeared on the cover of U.S. News & World Report, which excerpted the book.

In a telephone interview Tuesday before broadcast of the pre-recorded interview, Ames said he believed he had been put in a cell known as the "hole" because he appeared on the cover of the magazine, Nightline reported.

The program's anchor, Ted Koppel, said one theory was that Ames had been placed in special custody for fear he might be harmed by an inmate angered at the new disclosures. Another possibility was that someone in the federal government had read the excerpts and it could be "payback time," he said.
The federal Bureau of Prisons did not return a phone call seeking comment on any change in the status of Ames's detention.
